parakeet: The Bible does not solve the morality problem. If it did, prisons wouldn't be filled with believers and churches would be immune from immorality. Christians often argue that nonbelievers cannot have an objective standard for morality because we lack God as the anchor. Now they claim that without God, people are left to human opinion, human limitation, and human wisdom. But that criticism collapses under the weight of the Bible itself, because the Bible is inescapably a human text. It's a collection of writings produced by ancient people with limited knowledge, limited perspective, cultural bias, tribal interest, and moral blind spots. So when Christians accuse non-believers of relying on the wisdom of human beings, they're describing their own system. It's the pot calling the kettle black. The difference is that they rename human words as divine speech. They call the alleged words of Moses, Matthew, Mark, Luke, John, Paul, and Peter the words of God. Basically any voice that gets approved to be included in their canon becomes God's voice. That's an interesting trick. If goodness means reducing harm, protecting the vulnerable, telling the truth, and increasing well-being, then the biblical record creates serious problems. Because the same God called good drowns the world, orders massacres, sanctions slavery, threatens eternal punishment, and demands worship under threat. That moral pattern does not stay in Scripture, my friends. It spills into society. Because when people are trained to treat cruelty as righteous, whenever it is attached to sacred authority, they become vulnerable to doing the same thing with human power. When cruelty rises in the form of a leader wrapped in religious language, nationalist symbolism or tribal importance, large numbers of believers always rush to sanctify it, rationalize it, or call it necessary every single time. Not because they have carefully measured its effects on human beings, but because the figure has already been framed as chosen, anointed on our side are necessary for the cause. And once a figure is framed that way, many believers stop using harm, justice, and well being as their standard. They switch to defense, excuse making, and loyalty. That pattern applies to both the Bible and to modern politics. The reason believers can read morally disturbing things in scripture and still call God good is the same reason many of them can watch human rulers behave in cruel, exploitative, dishonest, or openly harmful ways and still call them righteous, chosen, or necessary. The issue is not just that they have a flawed moral conclusion.
